title: When AI Levels the Playing Field: Skill Homogenization, Asset Concentration, and Two Regimes of Inequality
author: Xupeng Chen · Shuchen Meng

kp.k: Task equalization can coexist with greater aggregate inequality
kp.d: Chen and Meng develop a cross-domain, task-based theoretical framework connecting AI-driven performance compression to concentrated returns on proprietary data, compute, distribution networks and organizational capabilities. Their four-link mechanism comprises skill homogenization, changing education returns, credential inflation and asset concentration. They explicitly characterize the later links as conditional model predictions, not established causal findings, and do not establish which inequality regime the economy occupies.
qs: We call this the inequality paradox  of AI.
The model thus identifies the  mechanism, not the verdict.

kp.k: Additive AI reduces relative, not absolute, output dispersion
kp.d: The central specification gives workers an ability-independent AI output floor while retaining their human-capital contribution. Adding this common floor raises mean output without changing its variance, reducing the coefficient of variation and delivering larger proportional gains to less-skilled workers. The authors stress that whether this production specification describes real AI use is an empirical question. This is a within-task result, not an automatic prediction about occupational wage dispersion.
qs: The expert still outperforms the novice (hi ϕ(z) remains), but AI narrows the gap  by adding a common floor.
adding a constant raises the mean without changing  variance.

kp.k: Reported experiments support compression within AI's capability frontier
kp.d: The paper reports customer-support evidence from Brynjolfsson et al. involving 5,179 agents, with novice resolution-rate gains of 35 percent and top performers unchanged; writing evidence from Noy and Zhang involving 444 participants and roughly 40 percent quality-distribution compression; and Peng et al.'s coding experiment involving 95 participants, with completion 56 percent faster and larger gains for less-experienced developers. These are findings attributed to existing studies, not new experiments by Chen and Meng. The evidence map separately reports the novice-support gain as +34%.
qs: GitHub Copilot users complete coding tasks 56 percent  faster, with larger gains for less experienced developers [Peng et al., 2023].
Homogenization is real within AI’s capability boundary; outside it, AI can widen gaps.

kp.k: Complementary analytical tasks can amplify experienced practitioners' advantages
kp.d: The authors distinguish substitutable generative tasks from complementary analytical tasks and cite Dell’Acqua et al. for evidence that AI can harm less-capable workers through over-reliance outside its competence frontier. Their broader CES analysis predicts compression for substitutes, neutrality for Cobb–Douglas production and divergence for complements. Complex legal strategy is explicitly included among complementary tasks; the paper does not present a legal-sector empirical test.
qs: The complement case (ρ < 0) describes analytical tasks—medical dif-  ferential diagnosis, complex legal strategy, architectural system design—where AI amplifies  experienced practitioners’ judgment rather than providing an independent substitute.

kp.k: Education returns shift conditionally rather than uniformly decline
kp.d: The model predicts falling returns to codifiable cognitive skills and rising relative returns to social, organizational and judgment skills when tasks are sufficiently substitutable, specifically σ > 1. Education responds through changing task prices rather than directly to the additive AI payment. The calibration does not establish the necessary substitution condition: σ is estimated at 1.166 with SE 1.639 and bootstrap 95% CI [0.246, 5.000]. Direct AI-specific evidence on education premia is unavailable.
qs: The prediction is not that education becomes worthless.
The sign of the education response depends on σ, which is an unresolved empirical
This  link has no direct test yet.

kp.k: Credential inflation is an untested screening-response prediction
kp.d: The model proposes that AI-assisted outputs become less informative about underlying ability, leading employers to place greater weight on credentials rather than direct performance assessment. Requirements and credential acquisition can consequently rise without greater task complexity. Earlier recession-related credential changes supply analogies, not evidence of the AI mechanism. A proposed screening-regime switch predicts a discrete increase in requirements when AI capability crosses an assessment threshold; testing requires post-2023 job postings linked to actual adoption.
qs: This section derives a testable prediction, not an explanation of observed credentialing trends.
firms  raise credential requirements not because AI makes jobs harder, but because AI makes talent  harder to identify.
This is the weakest link.

kp.k: Proprietary versus commodity AI determines asset-return direction
kp.d: The firm-side model distinguishes data, compute and organizational capital, aggregated into one complementary-asset index for tractability. Its two-sector microfoundation predicts rising effective asset elasticity only when the AI production channel is more capital-intensive than traditional production, ψ > η0. If commodity or open-source diffusion instead lowers ψ below η0, the concentrating channel reverses. This technology-structure condition is a proposed empirical test, not a validated account of current markets.
qs: the AI channel is more capital-intensive than tradi-  tional production.
When AI is commoditized via open-source (ψ < η0 ), η̃ ′ (A) < 0 and the concentrating          channel reverses.

kp.k: Baseline concentration is not an explosive accumulation process
kp.d: At the calibrated values η1 = 0.323 and γL = 0.55, the profit elasticity η/(1−γL) is approximately 0.72, below the model's self-reinforcement threshold of 1. The authors therefore interpret concentration as a level effect rather than explosive proportional divergence. They discuss crossing the threshold over a 10–20 year horizon as a possibility rather than an observed development.
qs: The widening        of firm differences is a level effect, not an explosive dynamic, at current parameter        values.
The explosive regime is not the current reality but a risk on the        horizon.

kp.k: Rent-sharing connects firm assets to worker wage inequality
kp.d: An illustrative worker–firm assignment framework separates firm wage premia, within-firm human-capital returns and their covariance. Under proprietary AI and the stated matching assumptions, asset-rich firms' rent-sharing premia rise, ability gradients fall and ability-based sorting weakens. Net wage inequality depends on whether increased between-firm dispersion outweighs within-firm compression and reduced sorting. The framework sketches rather than solves equilibrium assignment.
qs: Meanwhile, the base premium ψj grows, meaning  all workers prefer high-K firms, but the ability-based sorting weakens.
This sketch does not solve the full equilibrium assignment problem

kp.k: Calibration illustrates mechanisms without independently identifying inequality's sign
kp.d: The Method of Simulated Moments exercise matches six targets to five structural parameters, holding rent-sharing ξ at 0.20. It produces a within-task CV reduction of 0.345, wage-compression ratio of 0.792 and aggregate ΔGini of +0.0050; the reported J-statistic is 0.036 with p = 0.849. However, aggregate Gini change is itself a calibration target. The sensitivity decomposition finds that the other five moments identify channel rates but have near-zero net influence on the aggregate sign. Dropping the Gini target yields ΔGini = −0.009. These are scenario-conditioned model outputs, not causal estimates.
qs: Only m6 has substantial  boundary influence (pass-through ≈ 1.0).
The model-implied Gini effect is +0.005, coexisting with substantial skill compression (21%  CV reduction)—a consequence of ξ = 0.20, not a robust finding.

kp.k: Institutional and technology parameters independently cross the regime boundary
kp.d: The standard 1,000-replication bootstrap gives a ΔGini 95% interval of [−0.0148, +0.0264], spanning both regimes. At otherwise calibrated values, varying ξ from 0.07 to 0.25 changes ΔGini from −0.0119 to +0.0153, crossing zero near 0.17. Holding ξ = 0.20, varying post-AI asset elasticity independently changes the sign near η1 ≈ 0.29. Illustrative proprietary-AI scenarios range from +0.0218 for tech/AI platforms to −0.0258 for education/government; these are model scenarios, not measured industry outcomes.
qs: varying ξ alone flips the sign,  but so does varying η1 alone.
The inequality effect depends  on the interaction of AI’s supply structure and labor market institutions.

kp.k: Occupational regressions cannot test within-task causal predictions
kp.d: The authors merge BLS OEWS May 2019 and May 2023 wages with Felten et al.'s AIOE index for 635 matched six-digit occupations. In 2023, the exposure coefficient on log(p90/p10) falls from 0.1088 to 0.0339 after controls. In first differences it falls from 0.0167 to a statistically insignificant 0.0099 with major-group fixed effects. Mean change in log(p90/p10) is −0.102. The authors treat these regressions as diagnostic rather than causal: occupations bundle heterogeneous tasks, exposure does not measure adoption and the period covers only early generative-AI diffusion.
qs: The regressions below are diagnostic, not confir-  matory: they document this mismatch.
The  AIOE index measures exposure potential
Neither design identifies a causal effect

kp.k: Testing requires task outputs, adoption measures and linked panels
kp.d: The proposed research agenda tests performance compression, conditional education-premium changes, credential inflation, within-/between-firm wage decomposition, concentration of AI investment and profits, and cross-market inequality regimes. Suggested designs include occupational OEWS/CPS panels, matched employer–employee data with firm adoption measures and Lightcast job-posting panels, including prospective 2015–2028 windows. The authors emphasize actual usage, task composition and time variation, with staggered-adoption estimators where appropriate; the requisite within-occupation, within-task data do not yet exist at scale.
qs: credible  tests require time variation in AI adoption, not just cross-sectional exposure indices.
These predictions should be tested jointly with task  composition data, not extrapolated from the aggregate calibration alone.

kp.k: Policy implications remain conditional on omitted equilibrium effects
kp.d: The model identifies credential-screening waste, market-power distortions and human-capital misallocation. It suggests that reducing complementary-asset concentration and promoting open-source diffusion shift outcomes toward equalization, whereas restricting AI capability impedes the equalizing channel without addressing concentration. The authors explicitly stop short of evaluated policy recommendations: their partial-equilibrium framework omits full goods-market closure, endogenous task creation, AI investment decisions, entry dynamics and innovation incentives.
qs: We do not claim general equilibrium closure.
These are  scenario-conditional model implications, not evaluated policy recommendations.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chen and Meng propose that AI can equalize task performance while increasing aggregate inequality through concentrated complementary assets; they present conditional mechanisms rather than a verdict on inequality.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain economic paper, not a study of legal services. The authors claim that an ability-independent AI output floor reduces relative performance dispersion on substitutable tasks, with larger proportional gains for lower-ability workers. They predict that returns to education bifurcate: codifiable cognitive skills lose value while complementary social, organizational and judgment skills gain value, conditional on task substitution. They also predict credential inflation as AI-assisted work becomes less informative for employer screening. On the firm side, proprietary, capital-intensive AI raises returns to concentrated data, compute and organizational assets, potentially increasing between-firm wage inequality even as within-firm dispersion falls. Commodity AI can reverse that concentrating channel. Their assignment sketch predicts weaker ability-based sorting alongside greater premiums for employment at asset-rich firms. Complex legal strategy appears only as an example of an analytical task where AI may complement experienced judgment, not as evidence about the legal profession.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors combine published task-performance evidence with a calibrated structural model, while explicitly distinguishing untested mechanisms from empirical findings.
pts.d: For task homogenization, Chen and Meng cite customer-support evidence from Brynjolfsson and colleagues, a writing experiment by Noy and Zhang, and a coding experiment by Peng and colleagues. As reported in this paper, these show approximately 35% productivity gains for novice support agents versus little change for top performers, roughly 40% compression in writing quality, and 56% faster coding-task completion. These are supporting studies, not new experiments by Chen and Meng. Dell’Acqua and colleagues supply the qualification that AI can hurt performance outside its capability frontier. Education-return changes lack direct AI-specific evidence; credential inflation relies on analogies with earlier technology shocks and remains untested. Firm-concentration evidence comes from existing research on AI adoption, firm growth, market concentration and between-firm wages, rather than causal validation of the full proposed chain. The authors fit five parameters to six moments using Method of Simulated Moments. The baseline simulated Gini change is +0.005, but aggregate Gini change is itself a calibration target; the other five moments identify mechanism rates rather than the aggregate sign. Dropping that target yields −0.009. The reported fixed-rent-sharing bootstrap interval spans −0.0148 to +0.0264. Their separate BLS OEWS/AIOE analysis covers 635 occupations in 2019 and 2023; the first-difference association becomes statistically insignificant after major occupation-group controls and is not offered as causal confirmation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most predictions are comparative-static and conditional on task substitutability, AI supply structure, asset concentration and rent-sharing, rather than dated forecasts.
pts.d: Homogenization applies within AI-capable tasks, not automatically across entire occupations; analytical or complementary tasks may instead show widening performance gaps. Education-premium decline requires a task substitution elasticity above one, which the calibration does not establish: its reported 95% interval is 0.246–5.000. Credential inflation requires the proposed degradation of screening signals and should be tested with post-2023 postings linked to actual adoption. The concentrating regime requires proprietary AI to be more capital-intensive than traditional production, together with sufficient asset concentration and rent-sharing. At baseline parameters, changing rent-sharing across 0.07–0.25 reverses the simulated inequality sign near 0.17; changing post-AI asset elasticity independently crosses the boundary near 0.29. The current calibrated profit elasticity is approximately 0.72, below the model’s self-reinforcing threshold of one. The authors discuss possible self-reinforcing concentration over a 10–20-year horizon as a risk, not a current finding. They regard 2019–2023 as too early to identify sustained generative-AI wage effects and propose future panels extending to 2028. The framework lacks full general-equilibrium closure and endogenous task creation, entry and AI investment decisions; its policy implications are scenario-conditional.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ across workers, applicants, educational investments, firms and economies; the paper does not establish legal-market-specific outcomes.
pts.d: Novices and lower-ability workers gain more proportionally on substitutable tasks, while experienced practitioners may benefit more on analytical tasks requiring judgment. Students and workers face changing returns to different kinds of education. Applicants may face higher credential requirements even without greater job complexity, while employers face a less informative screening environment. Asset-rich firms gain relative to asset-poor competitors under proprietary AI, and rent-sharing passes some of those advantages to their employees. The model therefore makes employer affiliation more important to wages even while some individual skill differences become less important. Industry scenarios illustrate different outcomes: tech/AI platforms have a simulated Gini increase of about 0.022, versus a decline of about 0.026 for education/government. A Scandinavia-like scenario combines stronger rent-sharing with lower asset concentration and yields about −0.010. These are parameterized scenarios, not observed industry or country effects. No distinct predictions are established for law-firm staffing, legal fees, clients or access to justice.
